description: The value of sportsmanship and the reasons performers turn to gamesmanship or deviance.
content_html:
How Performers Are Expected to Behave

Sport is governed not only by written rules but by unwritten codes of conduct that define how athletes are expected to treat opponents, officials and the spirit of competition itself. These codes range from formal customs to cultural expectations, and they are often tested most severely when the pressure to win is at its greatest. Understanding the difference between behaviour that upholds sporting values and behaviour that exploits or undermines them is central to sport’s identity as more than a simple contest of skill.

Etiquette

Etiquette refers to the unwritten rules of conduct in sport — customs that participants are expected to follow even though they are not written into the official rule book. In tennis, it is considered etiquette to acknowledge a lucky net cord with a gesture to your opponent. In golf, players are expected to repair divots, rake bunkers and maintain silence when others are playing. In cricket, a fielding side traditionally applauds a departing batsman who has played well. None of these behaviours are compulsory under the laws of the game, but failing to observe them draws social disapproval and signals a disrespect for the sport’s traditions.

Sportsmanship

Sportsmanship describes behaviour that embodies fair play, respect and generosity in competition. A sportsmanlike act might include a footballer kicking the ball out of play when an opponent is injured so they can receive treatment, despite there being no rule requiring it. It includes shaking hands with opponents after a match, accepting officials’ decisions without complaint, and refusing to take advantage of an opponent’s misfortune. Sportsmanship is widely seen as a moral standard to which all competitors should aspire, regardless of the stakes.

Key Fact

Etiquette is the unwritten code of conduct in a sport (customs and traditions). Sportsmanship is the attitude and behaviour of fair play, respect and generosity towards opponents and officials. Both go beyond the written rules and reflect the spirit of competition.

Gamesmanship

Gamesmanship sits at the opposite end of the conduct spectrum from sportsmanship. It involves using strategies that are technically within the rules but deliberately break their spirit to gain an unfair advantage. Examples include: a tennis player bouncing the ball an excessive number of times before serving in order to disrupt an opponent’s concentration; a rugby player deliberately slowing play by lying on the wrong side of a ruck for as long as the referee will allow; or a batsman calling for a new bat purely to break the bowling side’s rhythm when momentum is building. Gamesmanship is legal but widely considered unsporting.

Gamesmanship is distinguishable from outright cheating because it stays within the formal rules. Cheating — such as deliberately handling the ball in football or falsifying a time in athletics — breaks the written rules and can result in disqualification. Gamesmanship breaks the spirit but not the letter of the law. However, the boundary is contested. At what point does prolonged time-wasting become a cynical act that undermines the sport? At what point does verbal distraction (sledging in cricket) cross from psychological contest into intimidation? These questions generate rich material for extended-response questions because they have no simple answers.

Deviance in Sport

Deviance in sport refers to behaviour that goes against the accepted norms and values of sporting competition. Unlike gamesmanship (which stays within the rules) and etiquette breaches (which are a matter of custom), deviance typically involves a more serious violation of sporting or social norms. Examples of deviant behaviour include: using performance-enhancing drugs; deliberately injuring an opponent; match-fixing; and persistent verbal abuse of officials.

OCR identifies three main reasons why performers engage in deviant behaviour. First, the desire to gain an unfair advantage: in a highly competitive environment where the margins between success and failure are tiny, some performers are willing to break the rules if they believe it will increase their chances of winning. Second, peer pressure: within certain sporting cultures, deviant practices (such as aggressive fouling or using banned substances) may be normalised to the point where an individual feels pressured to conform in order to be accepted by teammates or coaches. Third, a win-at-all-costs culture: when winning is prioritised above all other values — by athletes, coaches, clubs or the media — the ethical boundaries that constrain behaviour are gradually eroded. Financial incentives at elite level can amplify this: the prize money, sponsorship and status attached to winning creates intense pressure to succeed at any cost.

Key Fact

Three reasons for deviance in sport: (1) to gain an unfair advantage over opponents; (2) peer pressure within a sporting culture that normalises unethical behaviour; (3) a win-at-all-costs culture driven by financial rewards, media pressure and the status attached to success.

Students often use etiquette and sportsmanship interchangeably, and confuse both with deviance. They are distinct concepts. Etiquette is sport-specific customs (how you are expected to behave in that particular sport). Sportsmanship is a broader moral attitude about how you treat opponents and the spirit of competition across all sport. Deviance is behaviour that violates norms and values — it is a more serious concept than a lapse of etiquette or even an act of gamesmanship. In a 6-mark question, use all three terms accurately: describe the etiquette of a specific sport (e.g. kicking the ball out in football when an opponent is injured), describe sportsmanship as a general value (e.g. shaking hands after the match), and distinguish deviance as a normative violation — not just poor manners, but a rejection of sporting values altogether.

The Value of Sportsmanship

These concepts matter beyond individual events. Sport’s social and cultural value rests partly on its reputation as an arena in which effort, skill and fair competition determine outcomes. When gamesmanship becomes widespread, public trust in sport erodes. When deviance is normalised, sport loses its role as a model of positive values for young participants. Research into youth sport suggests that the conduct of elite athletes influences the attitudes of young people who aspire to perform at a high level. Athletes who model sportsmanship — acknowledging good play by opponents, respecting officials, competing without cynicism — provide a more powerful form of influence than those who win by any means necessary.
exam_tip_html: For a 3 marks — Describe question on etiquette, students often give one-word answers like “etiquette means respect.” To earn 3 marks, describe the concept fully (what it is), give a specific sporting example, and explain why it matters. For a 6 marks — Analyse question, avoid listing definitions. Instead, analyse how sportsmanship, gamesmanship and deviance each shape the experience of sport for different groups — performers, officials and young participants. A critical OCR-specific distinction: deviance is on the OCR spec as a separate term from gamesmanship. Be clear that deviance violates sporting norms and values (it goes further than simply bending the rules), and always give the three OCR reasons (unfair advantage, peer pressure, win-at-all-costs culture) when asked to explain why performers behave deviantly.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Etiquette is the unwritten code of conduct in a sport (customs and traditions); sportsmanship is the broader moral attitude of fair play, respect and generosity towards opponents and officials.
  • Gamesmanship exploits loopholes within the rules to gain a psychological or tactical advantage — it is within the rules but against their spirit, and widely considered unsporting.
  • Deviance is behaviour that violates the norms and values of sport. OCR identifies three reasons: gaining unfair advantage, peer pressure, and win-at-all-costs culture driven by financial reward and media pressure.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes gamesmanship?
A) Behaviour that involves physically harming an opponent to gain advantage
B) Strategies that break the formal rules of the sport to achieve a result
C) Actions that are within the rules but deliberately violate the spirit of competition
D) Behaviour that shows respect and generosity towards opponents
practice_questions.marks: C) Actions that are within the rules but deliberately violate the spirit of competition [1 mark]

1 mark for a basic definition identifying fair play, respect or generosity; 1 mark for linking this to treatment of opponents, officials or the rules of the sport. Example full-mark answer: 'Sportsmanship is behaviour that shows fair play, respect and generosity towards opponents, officials and the rules of the sport, placing the spirit of competition above personal gain.'

practice_questions.text: State two examples of etiquette from two different sports.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for two distinct examples from different sports. Examples: tennis player acknowledging a net cord to their opponent (1); golfer repairing a divot or raking a bunker (1); cricketer applauding a well-played innings by an opposition batsman (1); rugby player helping an opponent to their feet after a tackle (1); footballer kicking the ball into touch when an opponent is injured (1). Two examples from the same sport describing the same type of behaviour score only 1 mark.

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by 'etiquette' in sport and give one specific sporting example.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for identifying etiquette as unwritten rules or informal codes of conduct (not part of the official rule book); 1 mark for explaining that etiquette involves customs or traditions expected of participants; 1 mark for a valid specific sporting example. Example full-mark answer: 'Etiquette is the unwritten code of conduct expected of performers in sport (1). It consists of customs and traditions that are not part of the official rules but that participants are expected to follow to show respect for the sport and its opponents (1). For example, in tennis it is expected that a player will gesture to acknowledge a lucky net cord, even though there is no rule requiring this (1).'

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why performers might engage in deviant behaviour in sport. Give a sporting example in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks (2 marks per reason, must give 2 distinct reasons; 1 mark for the reason, 1 mark for development or example).
Acceptable reasons: to gain an unfair advantage (1) - for example, a power athlete using anabolic steroids to increase muscle mass and improve performance in competition (1); peer pressure within a sporting culture that normalises unethical behaviour (1) - for example, a young player who adopts aggressive fouling tactics because it is normalised and rewarded within their club culture (1); a win-at-all-costs culture driven by financial rewards, sponsorship or media pressure (1) - for example, a professional player who feigns injury to waste time and secure a narrow lead because the financial incentive of winning outweighs ethical concerns (1).

practice_questions.text: A county-level netball player watches her team's opponents using repeated gamesmanship during a closely contested match, including deliberate time-wasting on restarts and persistent verbal comments designed to distract players at set pieces. Analyse the impact this behaviour might have on the match, the performers involved and the wider sport.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained analysis across all three areas (match, performers, wider sport). Points are developed with specific examples from a sporting context. The distinction between gamesmanship and deviance is maintained. Uses accurate vocabulary (etiquette, sportsmanship, deviance, spirit of competition). Continuous analytical prose rather than a list.

Secure: Covers at least two of the three areas with developed points; mostly accurate; mostly applied to a sporting context.

Developing: Relevant points present but limited development; may address only one area; minimal sporting context.

Emerging: Basic observations that gamesmanship is bad; no development or application.

Acceptable points:
On the match: time-wasting reduces the quality of play and genuine competition time (negative); it may frustrate the opposition into making errors or receiving cautions (tactical gain for the gamesmanship team).
On the performers: players receiving gamesmanship may feel demoralised, distracted or become aggressive in response (negative); players using gamesmanship risk losing focus on their own game (self-harm); young performers may normalise this as acceptable behaviour (wider harm to sport culture).
On the wider sport: frequent gamesmanship erodes the spectator experience and reduces public enjoyment (negative); it undermines sport's role as a model of positive values for young participants (social harm); officials face greater difficulty managing the game (increased pressure on officiating); if it becomes culturally accepted, the spirit and values of netball are undermined long-term.

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is an example of gamesmanship rather than sportsmanship?
options: Shaking hands with opponents after a match
Kicking the ball out when an opponent is injured
Bouncing the ball excessively before serving to disrupt a nervous opponent
Applauding a good shot by your opponent

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following best describes deviance in sport?
options: Customs expected of participants that are not in the rule book
Behaviour showing fair play and respect for opponents
Tactics within the rules but against their spirit
Behaviour that violates the norms and values expected of participants

knowledge_checks.q: Etiquette refers to the _____ rules or informal codes of behaviour expected of performers in sport.
One reason performers engage in deviance is a win-at-all-costs _____, which erodes the ethical boundaries of sporting competition.
Match each term to its correct description:
right: Unwritten customs and traditions specific to a sport
Fair play, respect and generosity towards opponents
Behaviour that violates the accepted norms and values of sport

flashcard_questions.a: Unwritten rules and customs expected of performers, beyond the official rules.
An attitude of fair play, respect and generosity towards opponents, officials and the spirit of competition.
Tactics within the rules but against their spirit, used to gain a psychological advantage.
Behaviour that violates the accepted norms and values expected of participants in sport.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one example of etiquette in tennis.
flashcard_questions.a: Acknowledging a lucky net cord with a gesture to your opponent.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one example of sportsmanship in football.
flashcard_questions.a: Kicking the ball out of play when an opponent is injured so they can receive treatment.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one example of gamesmanship in tennis.
flashcard_questions.a: Bouncing the ball excessively before serving to disrupt an opponent's concentration.

flashcard_questions.q: Is gamesmanship the same as cheating?
flashcard_questions.a: No — gamesmanship is within the formal rules; cheating breaks the written rules.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the three OCR reasons for deviant behaviour in sport.
flashcard_questions.a: To gain an unfair advantage; peer pressure; a win-at-all-costs culture.

flashcard_questions.q: What happens when gamesmanship becomes widespread in sport?
flashcard_questions.a: Public trust erodes and sport loses its value as a model of positive social behaviour.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does peer pressure lead to deviance in sport?
flashcard_questions.a: Unethical practices are normalised within a sporting culture, pressuring individuals to conform.

glossary_terms.definition: The unwritten rules or informal codes of behaviour expected of participants in a sport, distinct from the formal written rules.
Behaviour that shows fair play, generosity and respect for opponents, officials and the rules of the sport.
The use of strategies that are within the letter of the rules but violate their spirit, intended to gain a psychological or tactical advantage over an opponent.
Behaviour in sport that violates the accepted norms and values expected of participants, often motivated by the desire for unfair advantage, peer pressure or a win-at-all-costs culture.
The principle that all competitors should have an equal chance to succeed, achieved by respecting the rules, officials and opponents throughout competition.
A sporting environment in which winning is prioritised above ethical values, creating pressure on performers to use any means necessary to succeed.

hero_image_caption: The values of sportsmanship, gamesmanship and deviance sit on a spectrum that defines how performers uphold or undermine the spirit of sport.
